articles.title_zh: Iron ore price nears one-week high on short-covering, China restocking bets
articles.content_orig:
Iron ore prices rebounded on Wednesday, supported by short-covering and expectations that steelmakers in top consumer China will begin restocking ahead of the Lunar New Year holiday.
The most-traded iron ore contract on China’s Dalian Commodity Exchange DCIOcv1 closed daytime trade up 1.56% at 682 yuan ($102.01) a metric ton after a 0.7% fall on Tuesday. It earlier touched its highest since October 29 at 685 yuan.
The benchmark December iron ore SZZFZ6 on the Singapore Exchange climbed 1.27% to its strongest since October 29 at $91.85 a ton, as of 0732 GMT.
Steel mills are expected to replenish ore inventories before the Lunar New Year holiday, providing near-term support to prices, analysts at Guoxin Futures said in a note.
Chinese steelmakers typically build seaborne iron ore stocks in the fourth quarter to meet production needs during the weeklong holiday period, which falls in February next year.
“Iron ore fundamentals remained weak, but a level at around $90 a ton created a strong technical support, limiting further downside room,” said Jiang Mengtian, an analyst at consultancy Horizon Insights.
While seaborne ore supply is expected to increase in the fourth quarter, analysts at Macquarie said “lower domestic iron ore output in China has partly offset the impact”.
Coking coal DJMcv1 and coke DCJcv1, other steelmaking ingredients, extended losses on rising supply and subdued demand, down 0.98% and 0.48%, respectively.
Steel benchmarks on the Shanghai Futures Exchange gained ground. Rebar SRBcv1 added 0.2%, stainless steel SHSScv1advanced 0.88%, hot-rolled coil SHHCcv1rose 0.29% and wire rod SWRcv1 gained 1.44%.
($1 = 6.6856 Chinese yuan)
(Reporting by Amy Lv and Lewis Jackson; Editing by Subhranshu Sahu and Jochelle Mendonca)

articles.title_orig: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq futures whipsaw after Democrats take control of House, Senate
articles.title_zh: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq futures whipsaw after Democrats take control of House, Senate
articles.content_orig:
In a resounding rebuke of President Donald Trump and his Republican Party, Democrats will control both the House and Senate for the last two years of Trump’s presidency, cementing one of the strongest midterm showings for either party in decades. The Associated Press called the upper chamber for Democrats late on Tuesday, after the party’s candidates secured victories in battleground races across the map. The outlet later called control of the lower chamber in the early hours of Wednesday morning as Democrats picked up more than two dozen seats.
The milestone potentially sets up a new political dynamic in Washington. A President has not had to deal with a Congress completely controlled by the opposition party since the last two years of Barack Obama’s presidency. Congress now stands to be a true counterweight to the White House and its agenda.
Democrats needed to net four seats to claim the Senate majority—a tough task given the map this cycle clearly favored Republicans. But with wins in Texas , Ohio, North Carolina, Iowa, and Maine, Democrats achieved what most handicappers had treated as a long shot until just weeks before Election Day. Democrats in multiple toss-up Senate races managed to effectively harness a national mood against Trump, the economy and the Iran War to win in places initially deemed out of reach for the party. Outstanding Senate races in states like Michigan could potentially pad Democrats’ majority.
Read more : How Trump’s Approval Compares to Other Presidents Just Before the Midterms
The new Senate is likely to be led by Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, who will regain his title of Senate Majority Leader from Republican Senator John Thune of South Dakota. While some Democrats have criticized Schumer’s leadership as minority leader over the past two years, it’s not clear if any Senators are prepared to challenge his leadership before the next Congress convenes in January.
The size of a possible Democratic majority in the House is still unclear as votes in many states were still being tallied, but signs of a significant Trump-centered backlash were popping up all over the country Tuesday night, potentially setting up the party to come away with a double-digit majority. Strategists with both parties had predicted for months that Republicans were unlikely to hold onto the House, where they could only afford to lose three seats.
House Democrats have vowed to use a House majority to aggressively investigate Trump, his Administration, and his allies, as well as push policy proposals they campaigned on, including ending the Iran War, undoing Trump’s tariffs and lowering the cost of living.
Likely Democratic control of the House would also mean the end of Mike Johnson’s speakership, with Democrats likely set to rally behind their leader in the House, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, to replace him. Jeffries would be the first Black speaker in U.S. history. Read more: 10 Candidates Who Could Make History in the Midterms
Polls had been consistently pointing for months to the House flipping to Democrats. For well over a year, nearly every poll from a reputable pollster asking voters which party’s candidate they intended to support showed Democrats with a clear advantage. But Republicans managed to hold their own or do better in fundraising, especially in pivotal battlegrounds for control of the Senate. And some Democrats as recently as this past weekend were worried that they may somehow still come up short.
Republicans spent much of the year trying to make the best of a bad environment. They constantly claimed the polls were all off, that Trump could still turn out his coalition that remade the modern GOP, and that Democrats’ overconfidence could depress their own turnout.
As Election Day neared, Republicans moved into triage mode. While they initially had planned to go on the offense against incumbent Democrats, those ambitions quickly evaporated as they shifted funding away from flipping Democratic seats and toward shoring up Republicans in a wider array of districts.
By late Tuesday, as exit polls started to paint a picture of the national mood, there were signs that many polls had likely under-estimated Democrats’ strength heading into Election Day.
The new Democratic caucus in both chambers are poised to include many new faces, from those who ran as moderates to self-avowed democratic socialists who ran as much against centrist leaders like Jeffries than Trump. Now starts the messy business of this new majority figuring out what they plan to do with their power. Trump will certainly be watching closely.

articles.content_orig:
Democrats scored sweeping victories in the U.S. midterm elections on Wednesday, flipping key Republican-held seats in Congress and securing historic wins in traditionally conservative states, as voters delivered a setback to President Donald Trump.
The party was projected to gain control of both chambers of Congress, with victories across several battleground states threatening to constrain Trump's legislative agenda for the remaining two years of his presidency.
Here are some of the scenes from polling stations, campaign headquarters and election-night celebrations across the United States.
Among the biggest surprises was Texas, where Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton to become the state's first Democratic U.S. senator since 1988.
Fellow Democrat Gina Hinojosa also unseated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, becoming the state's first Latina governor and ending more than three decades of Republican control of the office.
In North Carolina, former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper flipped a Republican-held Senate seat after defeating Trump-backed Michael Whatley. Cooper will succeed retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who announced his departure after clashing with Trump over his tax and spending legislation.
In Georgia, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff secured reelection against Trump-backed Republican Mike Collins, while former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governor's race, becoming the first Black woman elected governor of a U.S. state.
Meanwhile, in Ohio, former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown staged a political comeback, defeating Republican incumbent Jon Husted in a closely watched Senate race.
The elections were widely viewed as a referendum on Trump's second term, with concerns over the cost of living, inflation and the war in Iran weighing on voter sentiment.
—CNBC's Danielle DeVries contributed to this article.

articles.title_orig: Treasury Yields Trade Lower, Decline May Not Persist Long Term
articles.title_zh: Treasury Yields Trade Lower, Decline May Not Persist Long Term
articles.content_orig:
Treasury yields moved lower on Wednesday as investors weighed big wins from Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield fell 3 basis points to 4.917%. The 30-year bond yield slid 4 basis points to 5.289%, and the shorter-term 2-year note yield declined marginally to 4.606%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.
Democrats obtained majorities in both the House and Senate . The party is projected to win at least 250 House seats and at least 54 in the Senate. Democrats flipped Senate seats from Republicans in Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, Maine and Texas. They also won key gubernatorial races in Ohio and Texas.
The resounding victory by Democrats could rein in government spending from the Trump administration, as it makes it harder for the White House to push legislation through Congress.
Traders at JPMorgan said one of the issues Wall Street is focusing on after the midterms is "reduced deficit spending."
"This can be achieved by asserting power over the budget and likely wading through a government shutdown," they said.

articles.title_orig: The Business Fallout From a Blue Wave
articles.title_zh: The Business Fallout From a Blue Wave
articles.content_orig:
Good morning. What do the U.S. midterm election results mean for finance leaders? With Democrats winning control of both chambers of Congress, companies could face greater scrutiny of issues such as AI investment and data center development. But the broader financing challenges facing finance chiefs extend beyond the shifting political landscape.
“CFOs should go into 2027 expecting sustained higher borrowing costs,” Josh Putnam, EY-Parthenon’s global and Americas corporate finance leader, told me. Financing conditions are also likely to remain volatile, regardless of which party controls Congress.
Growing deficits, strong capital demand, inflation volatility, and policy uncertainty are putting pressure on long-term rates, Putnam said, making disciplined capital allocation, debt management, and investment decisions increasingly important for finance chiefs.
His advice is to stress-test investment hurdles, evaluate debt maturities, and protect balance-sheet flexibility. Companies must understand which investments can generate returns above their cost of capital and redirect resources when they cannot, he said.
Political gridlock could add risk, but on its own it does not necessarily mean higher long-term borrowing costs.
A divided government “would not automatically push term premiums higher,” said Gregory Daco, EY-Parthenon’s chief economist. But repeated budget disagreements, shutdown risks, debt ceiling stress, and greater fiscal uncertainty “would reinforce upward pressure,” he said.
Daco recommends testing investments against a range of financing costs and maintaining hurdle rates that reflect a structurally higher and more volatile cost of capital.
For companies, however, the risks extend beyond long-term interest rates. Political uncertainty can also affect access to credit and the cost of short-term financing.
“Markets respond to uncertainty by charging more, whether the risk originates in Washington, D.C., or on Wall Street,” said Mark Williams, a master lecturer in finance at Boston University’s Questrom School of Business and a former bank examiner for the Federal Reserve Bank.
Williams said that banks react to elevated risk by tightening credit terms and reducing lending. “Legislative gridlock can create volatile funding cycles and cause short-term borrowing costs to spike,” he explained. Companies relying on commercial paper, a form of short-term corporate borrowing, should consider longer-term funding, diversify financing sources, and secure credit lines across multiple banks, he said.
Because a divided government can increase the risk of shutdowns, which can delay the release of economic data, CFOs should also develop internal models to fill those gaps, Williams said. Government contractors, meanwhile, should evaluate how potential payment delays could affect cash flow.
AI investment could face particularly intense financial scrutiny as financing costs rise and regulatory uncertainty increases. Voters on Tuesday sent a clear message about the AI buildout: the costs of data centers are now a political issue. Candidates in both parties who campaigned on rising electric bills won key races, and at least 14 Ohio towns passed restrictions on data center development, Fortune reported .
The results underscore the growing regulatory and political uncertainty facing AI and data center developers, which could drive up costs and complicate project financing, Williams said. Private credit funds, the primary lenders in the space, would demand higher interest rates, he said, and prices on outstanding AI bonds could fall as yields rise.
But the market was already recalibrating AI risk before the election, Williams noted. He recommends returning to corporate finance fundamentals, including more conservative net present value assumptions, multi-variable scenario analysis, and stress testing against higher borrowing costs and stricter lending covenants.
Daco also sees a political dimension. With affordability central to the election, “a backlash is likely if households see AI investment raising power costs while its benefits remain concentrated,” he said.
CFOs should prioritize projects with measurable productivity gains, account fully for power and infrastructure costs, and pair technology investment with investment in workers and skills, Daco said.
The financial discipline required to navigate the next economic cycle remains vital. As Putnam put it, “Companies that demonstrate they can put capital to work effectively will be best positioned to pursue growth.”

articles.title_orig: Private companies added 86,000 jobs in October, slightly higher than expected, ADP says
articles.title_zh: Private companies added 86,000 jobs in October, slightly higher than expected, ADP says
articles.content_orig:
Private sector job growth held steady in October, with gains spread across sectors, as the labor market showed fresh signs of stabilization, ADP reported Wednesday.
The payrolls processing firm said companies added 86,000 jobs during the month, the same as the downwardly revised total for September and slightly ahead of the Dow Jones estimate for 75,000.
Employment gains came mainly in the service sector.
Trade, transportation and utilities led with 39,000 new jobs, while education and health services added 28,000, and leisure and hospitality contributed 19,000. Other sectors showing gains included financial activities (15,000), construction (13,000) and other services (10,000).
However, some of the gains were offset by a decline of 27,000 in professional and business services and a loss of 8,000 in natural resources and mining. Information services, a sector potentially impacted by the artificial intelligence buildout, lost 2,000 jobs.
Salaries continued to show gains, particularly for those changing jobs — those workers saw a 4.8% annual gain. A report Tuesday from the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed that the number of people quitting their job, a sign of labor market mobility, hit its highest level since March 2025.
Workers overall saw a 3.2% base pay gain, while gross pay increased 4.7% annually. Pay for those staying in their jobs rose 3%.
"Employers of all sizes were hiring last month, and our data suggests that job-changers were lured by a combination of bonuses, overtime, and more hours in addition to higher base pay," said ADP's chief economist, Nela Richardson. "Taken together, earnings growth for these workers hit its fastest pace since March 2024."
Companies with between 50 and 499 workers added 33,000 jobs. Large businesses added 24,000, while small firms increased rolls by 28,000.
The ADP report serves as a precursor to the BLS nonfarm payrolls count to be released Friday.
Economists surveyed by Dow Jones are looking for the BLS report for October to show a gain of 59,000 after September's modest growth of 29,000.

articles.title_orig: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook comes at a price
articles.title_zh: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook comes at a price
articles.content_orig:
People try out the new MacBook Pro with a touchscreen following the launch by Apple CEO John Ternus in Los Angeles, on Oct. 28, 2026. (REUTERS)
Apple has finally given the MacBook Pro something many people have wanted for years: a touchscreen. The company unveiled its first touchscreen MacBook Pro on Oct. 28, introducing a new way to interact with its laptop. It also brings a stunning OLED display, a thinner design and some serious processing power. However, there's one detail that might make you think twice before reaching for your wallet. The new touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $2,899.
That's a lot of money for a laptop, even by Apple's standards. So, what exactly are you getting for that price? More importantly, will touching your MacBook's screen make enough of a difference to justify an upgrade? Let's look at what Apple has introduced and who might benefit most.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

8 BIGGEST THINGS WE LEARNED FROM APPLE'S 2026 EVENT
Apple's first touchscreen MacBook Pro lets users interact directly with the display, bringing familiar iPhone and iPad gestures to the Mac. (Apple)
For years, Apple maintained that the Mac worked best with a keyboard and trackpad. Meanwhile, Windows laptop owners have enjoyed touchscreen options for a long time. Apple even experimented with touch controls through its Touch Bar, but that feature never replaced the traditional laptop experience.
Now Apple has changed course. Its new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display lets you interact directly with the screen. You can scroll through websites with your finger or pinch to zoom into photos. Apple also lets you drag content between windows and interact with supported creative apps.
Think about how often you instinctively touch your laptop screen, especially after spending years using an iPhone or iPad. Now that gesture will actually do something on the new MacBook Pro. Apple also redesigned the hinge to keep the display steadier when you touch it. That's a thoughtful addition because nobody wants a screen wobbling every time they tap a button.
However, this remains a traditional laptop. It doesn't fold into a tablet, and it doesn't support Apple Pencil. You'll still use the keyboard and trackpad for much of your work. That may disappoint anyone hoping to replace both a MacBook and an iPad with one device.
While everyone is talking about the touchscreen, Apple's new display technology might have an even greater impact on your everyday experience. The company calls it the PROLED XDR Display, and it uses tandem OLED technology. Unlike traditional laptop screens that rely on a backlight, OLED pixels produce their own light. That allows the display to show deep blacks alongside bright highlights without the same backlight glow.
Apple says the new screen reaches up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness for both HDR and SDR content. It also delivers a claimed 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio and supports refresh rates up to 120Hz for smoother motion. Those numbers sound impressive, but what will you actually notice?
Apple CEO John Ternus mingles at the launch of a new MacBook Pro with a touch screen in Los Angeles on Oct. 28, 2026. (REUTERS)
Photos should look more vibrant, especially when you're viewing pictures taken on your iPhone. Movies can show more detail in dark scenes. If you edit videos or work with photography, the improved color accuracy could be especially useful.
Apple has also added an antireflective coating to help reduce glare. An optional nano-texture finish provides additional reflection control for people who work in bright environments. For someone who spends hours looking at a laptop screen, these improvements could be more valuable than touch alone.
Apple isn't holding back on performance. The new touchscreen MacBook Pro comes with either an M5 Pro or M5 Max processor . Both target people who need more processing power than a basic laptop typically provides. If you're editing high-resolution video or working with large photo libraries, these chips are designed to handle that workload. Apple also offers configurations with up to 128GB of unified memory and 16TB of storage. However, those upgrades can drive the price considerably higher.
The new MacBook Pro runs macOS 27 and includes Apple Intelligence alongside Apple's upgraded Siri AI. It also brings Dynamic Island to the Mac for the first time. That familiar feature from the iPhone sits near the top of the display and gives you access to live updates and useful controls. For video calls, Apple includes a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera. Meanwhile, an upgraded six-speaker system promises deeper bass. The laptop also includes Thunderbolt 5 connectivity and an HDMI port, which should appeal to people connecting external displays.
12 BIGGEST APPLE WWDC 2026 TAKEAWAYS YOU NEED TO KNOW
Apple's new touchscreen MacBook Pro comes in 14-inch and 16-inch models, with prices starting at $2,899. (Apple)
One concern with touchscreen laptops is whether all that additional technology makes them heavier. Apple says it has managed to move in the opposite direction. The new 14-inch touchscreen MacBook Pro weighs about three pounds, roughly half a pound less than its predecessor. The 16-inch model comes in at four pounds, approximately 0.7 pounds lighter. Both models also feature slimmer designs. That should make carrying a MacBook Pro between meetings or packing one for a trip a little easier.
Apple promises up to 24 hours of battery life, depending on the configuration and usage. That's an impressive claim for a machine with this much performance and such a bright display. However, we'll need independent testing to see how battery life holds up during real-world work.
Apple has positioned its touchscreen MacBook Pro firmly in premium territory. The 14-inch model with the M5 Pro chip starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch version starts at $3,399. If you want the more powerful M5 Max processor, prices jump to $4,499 for the 14-inch model and $4,799 for the 16-inch version. And remember, those are starting prices for each configuration. Adding more memory or storage can increase the total substantially.
There is another important detail. Apple introduced a separate 14-inch MacBook Pro with its newer M6 chip on Oct. 27. That model starts at $1,999, but it uses a Liquid Retina XDR Display without touch support. That means you're looking at a $900 difference between Apple's entry-level M6 MacBook Pro and its least expensive touchscreen model. Of course, the more expensive version also includes an M5 Pro processor and the upgraded OLED display. These are different performance configurations, so the additional $900 doesn't represent the cost of touch alone.
For another perspective, the previous 14-inch MacBook Pro with the M5 Pro chip started at $2,499. That makes the new touchscreen version $400 more expensive than its comparable predecessor. Still, this gives you a meaningful choice. You can buy a powerful new MacBook Pro for considerably less if you don't need to interact directly with the screen. We've previously reported on how rising AI chip costs have pushed Apple prices higher. This latest introduction adds another premium option to an already expensive lineup.
Apple says many existing Mac apps will respond to touch immediately because macOS can translate finger taps into mouse clicks. That should make basic interaction straightforward, even before developers fully optimize their software.

articles.title_orig: Israel’s president accepts certified election results in a blow to Netanyahu’s claim of vote fraud
articles.title_zh: Israel’s president accepts certified election results in a blow to Netanyahu’s claim of vote fraud
articles.content_orig:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday accepted as legally binding the certified results from last week’s parliamentary elections and said he would begin consultations with party representatives on the formation of a new government.
Herzog’s acceptance of the results as valid dealt a blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s effort to discredit the vote in which his religious-nationalist bloc lost its majority in the Israeli parliament, or Knesset, while Arab-led parties made historic gains.
Netanyahu and his supporters have repeatedly made unsubstantiated claims that the Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, possibly with foreign assistance.
The Israeli president is required now to sit down with various party leaders to determine who to name as prime minister-designate — a process that could potentially bring Netanyahu’s opponents to power.
Israel’s election commission said earlier on Wednesday that after a thorough investigation of all parties’ claims of fraud it had found “no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results.”
Netanyahu’s Likud party did not respond to a request for comment.
A separate investigation by the Shin Bet intelligence service, which is headed by David Zini, a Netanyahu appointee and loyalist, into allegations of foreign interference in the election is still ongoing.
In a private meeting Wednesday of the election committee’s members, its head, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, read out an intelligence assessment from the Shin Bet saying the agency believed there had been a “widespread phenomenon involving the influx of substantial funds into Israel from foreign states,” including from countries hostile toward Israel.
The Shin Bet provided no evidence to explain its assertion. The Associated Press obtained a transcript of the assessment from a person who attended the meeting. The person requested anonymity to discuss a closed-door meeting.
The committee has previously said that while claims about foreign actors seeking to influence the election are serious and under investigation, it does not believe that any such interference affected the results — even if it had happened.
Sohlberg reiterated that stance on Wednesday.
“At this stage, these are merely suspicions, and even if they are substantiated, the scope of their potential impact is limited,” he said during a ceremony to present the certified election results to Herzog.
Sohlberg added that it was dangerous to cast doubt on the results and said they are legally binding.
Public trust in the electoral process is “easy to destroy, yet very difficult to repair,” he warned.
In the Oct. 27 vote, neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the bloc of allies of his chief rival, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, secured a parliamentary majority needed to form a new government, raising the possibility of an alliance between the two rivals or an alliance between Eisenkot and some of the Arab-led parties.
Israel’s president is now expected to begin a series of sit-downs with political parties. The meetings are expected to unfold over the next several days.
Herzog is then to choose the candidate — most likely Netanyahu or Eisenkot — who he believes is most likely to be able to form a coalition government, setting the stage for weeks of negotiations.
If neither man can put together a government, the country would hold a new election early next year.
The Shin Bet had requested approval from Israel’s attorney general on Tuesday to interrogate several elected officials as part of the agency’s separate probe, including the Ra’am party leader Mansour Abbas and other senior Arab lawmakers, Israeli media reported.
The request was sharply rejected.
“It is not permissible to interrogate citizens or elected officials without evidence to justify such action,” Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara said.
The Joint List of Arab parties condemned the request, calling it a “campaign of incitement” by Netanyahu and his allies designed to delegitimize the Arab vote.
A far-right ally of Netanyahu, Itamar Ben-Gvir, rejected the committee’s findings that the elections were valid.
He called on the Shin Bet, over which he has no jurisdiction, to “arrest all the leaders of the Arab political parties” and to interrogate them in “basement interrogation cells until these suspicions are fully clarified.”
Herzog said Wednesday that the Shin Bet investigation into possible foreign interference should play out. But he cautioned that Arab Israeli voters “must not be smeared.”
“I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently,” Herzog said.

One color dominates international headlines about the U.S. midterm election results . French newspaper Libération called the Democrats' win " une vague bleue ," or blue wave, Britain's Daily Mail dubbed it a "historic blue tsunami," and The Times of India's headline ran "midterm blues for Trump."
Countries at war were also watching closely, with Ukrainian newspaper The Kyiv Independent's online headline hopeful : "Democrats seize control of Congress in blow to Trump, potential boost for Ukraine."
Russia had a different take. Rossiyskaya Gazeta , the state-run daily newspaper, suggested the results would in fact be a blow to Ukraine, which has firm support from the European Union. "Brussels, brace yourself. After the Republicans' defeat, Trump's wrath will fall on Europe," read the headline.
In the Middle East, the Tehran Times put the Republicans' resounding defeat down to President Trump's decision to attack Iran earlier this year.
"The Iran war comes home to hit Trump at the ballot box," its headline read. The war, which Trump promised would be over quickly, has dragged on, sent oil prices soaring, and affected many Americans' daily lives with the affordability crisis.
And in Israel, which just held its own seismic elections last week, headlines focused on what the Democrats' victory means for the U.S. support of the Jewish state and its war in Gaza.
The Times of Israel ran a headline focusing on Democrat, and Muslim, candidate Abdul El-Sayed's triumph in the Michigan Senate race, saying "Anti-Israel El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate race, pledges no money for 'apartheid, genocide.'" The headline in Israel's other daily Haaretz read: "Abdul El-Sayed Shows Opposition to Israel Is No Barrier to Winning Battleground States."
Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks at an election night event, early Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, in Detroit. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP hide caption
The Toronto Star in Canada, which is in the midst of a contentious trade war with the U.S., called the results a "rebuke" to Trump. Across the southern border in Mexico, El Universal newspaper's headline was similar, reading simply: "Setback for Trump."
Many foreign leaders shied away from commenting directly on the results, as unlike a U.S. presidential election where they politely congratulate the winner, they see midterms as a domestic American issue.
However Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has an acrimonious relationship with Trump, was forthright on X.
"Yesterday, American society voted against policies that only impoverish. Against hate. Against machismo. Against climate denialism and against the privileges of the elites," Sánchez said.
In South Africa, where diplomatic relations with the U.S. are at an all-time low after Trump falsely accused the government of persecuting its white minority, President Cyril Ramaphosa said "The people of America have spoken."
Ramaphosa made the comments as he cast his own ballot in South Africa's municipal elections Wednesday, adding: "I do think that this is going to introduce a new era in world relations…. We're hoping that on a bilateral basis there will be a coming together of minds."
A senior Russia diplomat suggested the Democratic Party's return to power in both houses of Congress bode ill for U.S.-Russian relations. "The approach of the activist wing of the Democratic Party towards Russia is extremely negative. There's nothing new in that," said Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov in an interview with the state RIA-Novosti news service. Ryabkov also signaled there would be no grand shifts in Russian foreign policy as a result.
In Germany, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius congratulated Democrats on an "historic victory," adding that Berlin's commitment to cooperating with the administration in Washington remains unchanged. He stressed that Berlin will be reaching out to both Democrats and Republicans.
Iranian government supporters step on U.S. and Israeli flags during the annual rally marking the anniversary of the 1979 U.S. Embassy takeover, outside the former embassy in Tehran, Iran, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. Vahid Salemi/AP hide caption
Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere said the results are a "powerful political signal about a change of course among American voters." Speaking to Reuters, Stoere said "voices are now emerging in American politics that are closer to us than the president and the administration have stood for, for example on climate and environment, and in foreign policy and development aid policy."
There was no immediate reaction from UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, but London Mayor Sadiq Khan, who Trump has frequently sparred with, said on X: "Congratulations to Democrats on a huge victory last night. With a focus on hope, unity and supporting families with the cost of living - their campaign was a true rejection of the damaging and divisive politics of Donald Trump."
A spokeswoman for China's foreign ministry told a daily press conference that the midterm elections "are an internal affair of the United States." She added that "China is willing to continue working with the U.S. to…strengthen communication, properly manage differences, expand cooperation, and build a constructive, strategically stable China-U.S. relationship based on the principles of respect, fairness, and reciprocity."
Japan's top government spokesman, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told a press conference that Japan's alliance with the U.S. remains essential for global peace and stability, regardless of the outcome of midterm elections.
The alliance "remains the cornerstone of Japan's foreign and security policy" and is crucial to "maximizing its national interests" amid an increasingly volatile and uncertain global situation," he added.
Iran's Parliament Speaker and top negotiator Mohammad ‌Baqer Ghalibaf commented on X: "Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message. If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare."
For Israel, the US midterm results fall during a time of political uncertainty, amid coalition-building talks after Trump's ally, incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, lost his parliamentary majority in Oct. 27 Israeli elections. "In some ways Netanyahu lost two elections in the last week," said Israel-American analyst Mairav Zonstein.
Netanyahu's rivals seized on the midterm results. One Israeli opposition leader, Yair Golan, said the U.S. results reveal "just how toxic Netanyahu is among both Democrats and Republicans." Another, Yair Lapid, said the U.S. results "eliminate any possibility of a unity government led by Netanyahu."

articles.title_orig: Switch 1 & 2 Cartridges Under Threat As Key ROM Manufacturer Exits Business
articles.title_zh: Switch 1 & 2 Cartridges Under Threat As Key ROM Manufacturer Exits Business
articles.content_orig:
Macronix, one of Nintendo's key ROM manufacturers for physical game cartridges, is ceasing the production of ROM altogether.
This comes via analyst David Gibson who relayed the news from Macronix's latest financial release. According to the data, ROM products accounted for just 5% of the firm's overall revenue for Q3 2026, representing a stark decrease of 39% year-on-year.
It will now shift its focus over to NOR and eMMC memory chips instead, and will no longer report ROM sales separately in its future financial releases.
Gibson is keen to stress that Nintendo will have other partners to utilise when it comes to the production of cartridges, but this move may nevertheless accelerate the transition to digital game sales alongside Game-Key Cards.
Digital sales have already made up more than 60% of Nintendo's total sales during Q4 2026 and Q1 2027, but this tends to fluctuate based on major game releases.
It'll be interesting to see whether Nintendo itself addresses this development in its own financial release, which it due to drop this week on 5th November. Even if it doesn't acknowledge it in its own material, it seems likely that the question will arise in the company's usual Q&A session. We'll keep an eye out and relay its reaction and plans going forward.
For now, it's likely business as usual for Nintendo, but we'll be interested to see just how this affects the production of physical cartridges in the future and whether it will indeed accelerate the transition to digital.

articles.content_orig:

McDonald's ( MCD ) sales growth slowed in the third quarter as consumers faced a challenging economic backdrop and the fast food chain unveiled its growth strategy. The results showed that same-store sales grew by 1.5% year over year, a tick above the 1.4% growth Wall Street expected, according to Bloomberg estimates. In Q3 last year, McDonald's posted same-store sales growth of 3.6%.
In the US, the company posted a 0.2% decline in comparable sales, slightly narrower than the expected 0.5% drop. Data from Placer.ai showed visits to the Golden Arches declined from a year ago, but the company said customers spent more when they did go. Promotions in October led to some strength ahead of the holiday season. CEO Chris Kempczinski said the company is "encouraged by improvement as the quarter progressed following our intervention on value."
Revenue came in at nearly $7.2 billion, below expectations of $7.4 billion, alongside adjusted earnings of $3.57 per share, above the expected $3.40 per share.
Ahead of the results, BTIG analyst Peter Saleh said "lower-income challenges, disappointing promotions and overly crowded marketing calendars" were top concerns among franchisee operators in the quarter.
"Beverages were called out as a rare bright spot," he added, alluding to an energy drink McDonald's launched with Red Bull in September.
The company is also leaning into holiday offerings beginning on Nov. 3. McDonald's unveiled a limited-time lineup consisting of a cookie butter coffee or latte, a cranberry-infused Sprite drink, and a cranberry-flavored Red Bull energy drink.
Citi's Jon Tower shared a similar message in a note, writing, "We still have confidence in beverages as a broader platform, [and] another attempt at entry-level value should come in early '27."
The company named Skye Anderson, a 26-year McDonald's veteran, as president of McDonald's USA last quarter. Anderson is working on a new value menu for 2027 after franchisees and consumers didn't fully engage with the company's under-$3 offerings.
Anderson will play a key role in a new growth strategy as McDonald's makes a long-term bet on artificial intelligence, hand-breaded chicken, and a return of the 90s-style restaurant design to regain customers who left for other chains, like Burger King ( QSR ).
McDonald's said it plans to invest $8.5 billion through 2036 to support restaurant tech updates with rent relief and capital. It intends to deliver roughly $5 billion of that investment by 2030.
According to Saleh, franchisees' reactions to the NEXT growth strategy are mixed.
"Franchisees [are] highly skeptical that level of margin gain is possible, unconvinced a broad remodel program is needed, and noting very few details about cost and co-investment have been shared," Saleh wrote. "Without a significant reduction in build cost and more field-testing, we don't believe Project NEXT can proceed."
McDonald's operators are expected to update the restaurants' look and feel as part of a 10-year remodel cycle, per McDonald's, and Kempczinski said those costs typically add up to $400,000 to $450,000 per restaurant.
Deploying the suite of McDonald's productivity improvements will cost franchise operators an additional $800,000 per US restaurant. For international markets, it will run operators around $650,000 to $750,000.

Design software maker Canva is cutting 22% of its staff, amounting to 1,271 people, amid a growth slowdown.
The company’s co-founder and CEO, Melanie Perkins, in a note to employees said while Canva has scaled so far, it needs to change to address slowing growth.
“Over the past thirteen years, we’ve turned a dream in a pitch deck into a platform used by hundreds of millions of people. None of it would have been possible without the talent, imagination, and care of every single person who has been part of this journey. Yet success in our first chapter doesn’t guarantee success in the next. This has been our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade,” Perkins wrote.
Canva is reshuffling its organizational chart and merging its product, growth and platform teams to reduce communication friction. The company is also reducing “subspecialisation,” which means its employees might be asked to take up more responsibilities. The company is also moving towards hybrid work and asking people to work from an office a few days a week.
The company has been shipping its own AI models to reduce costs and reliance on third-party models, but it still had to cut its revenue growth forecast to 20% from 30% to address ballooning AI costs. This also resulted in Canva’s early investors cutting its valuation to about $35 billion earlier this year.
Canva is also facing increasing competition from AI startups and general-purpose chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini, whose image generation capabilities allow people to easily put together posters and presentations.

articles.title_orig: AI Data Center Boom Set for Upheaval After US Election Rout
articles.title_zh: AI Data Center Boom Set for Upheaval After US Election Rout
articles.content_orig:
AI data center stocks came under pressure as Democrats — seen as proponents of moratoriums on the buildout — won big in midterm elections and in key technology hubs like Texas.
Markets were already anticipating the Democrats to win the House of Representatives and possibly take Senate control. But the Texas governor mansion going to Democrats was a big blow, analysts said. Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who wants to enact an immediate moratorium on data centers in the state, won over incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott. According to Wells Fargo, 27% of planned data center gigawatts is in the Lone Star State.
The midterm elections will slow the pace of data center buildouts across the U.S., Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co., said in a note on Wednesday morning.
"There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control especially over the Senate will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next 2 years," he said.
He added that the election in Texas was the "biggest worry" of the night for tech investors and the AI trade because that's where around 25%-30% of data center gigawatts and capacity will come from.
Shares of Elon Musk 's SpaceX were down 4% after the open, and Tesla shares were down 5%. The Democrats' victory in Texas is a big setback for Musk , where he heavily backed Republican candidates, and where his companies Tesla and SpaceX are based. Musk spent a record of at least $474 million on the midterms and funneled $224 million into Texas alone, where Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott lost to Democrats.
SpaceX is currently building out multiple gigawatts of data center capacity, including projects in Texas.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said in a post on X in the early hours on Wednesday, referring to his speculative plans to build AI infrastructure off-planet.
Neoclouds CoreWeave and Iren fell by 4% in morning trading on Wednesday. Peer Nebius Group was down about 0.5% and Oracle was up 2%. Nvidia shares were slightly in the red.
Tech giants Alphabet , Meta and Microsoft mostly bucked the trend and were higher. Alphabet was up 3%, Amazon was up 7%, Meta was up 2%, and Microsoft was up 5.5%.
The Democratic win in Texas adds to existing pressure on the bull-market-leading AI trade. The Nasdaq-100 index fell into correction territory to end October as concerns mounted that the growth of data center spending by big hyperscalers and private AI juggernauts OpenAI and Anthropic was slowing.
"We believe the equity market reaction from the midterms mostly depends on the outcome of the Texas governor's race — a Dem win could potentially be a left-tail event to the AI trade, warned Ohsung Kwon, Wells Fargo's chief equity strategist, in a report this week.
Democrats won or retained the governorships in other key data center states Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio. Georgia represents 7% of all the planned U.S. datacenter gigawatts, while Ohio and Pennsylvania account for 5% apiece, estimates Wells Fargo.
Notable investment strategist Michael Hartnett of Bank of America warned earlier this year that Democrats winning the Senate, combined with taking the Texas governorship could lead to a "big slump" in stocks of more than 10% into year-end.
"Data centers went from being a popular economic development tool in 2024 and 2025 to something of a pariah by the time the midterm campaigns gathered steam," wrote the Washington policy team at Optimal Advisory this week. "The midterms are likely to send a message to local and state officials that there is a political upside to blocking, delaying and/or raising the cost of data centers."

Semiconductor stocks witnessed a brutal sell-off on Friday, Oct. 30, after Intel 's guidance came in well below expectations due to a declining personal computer (PC) market.
The PHLX Semiconductor Sector index fell 7% in a single session. Shares of Nvidia ( NVDA +2.29% ) were down more than 4% on Oct. 30, while other popular semiconductor stocks , such as Broadcom ( AVGO +3.07% ) and Micron Technology ( MU +2.58% ) , also pulled back substantially.
However, I think that the sell-off in this sector is overdone. That's because chips play a central role in various applications, including artificial intelligence (AI), smartphones, computers, vehicles, and factories. Bank of America estimates that the U.S. semiconductor industry's revenue alone could reach $3.2 trillion in 2030, up from an estimated $1.7 trillion this year.
As such, now is a good time to buy some top names in this sector following the recent pullback.
Image source: Getty Images.
Nvidia and Broadcom are among the top two semiconductor companies capitalizing on the AI-fueled chip demand. Both companies have been enjoying solid growth lately, and the good news is that they expect to sustain their momentum going forward.
NVDA Revenue (TTM) data by YCharts
Nvidia management, for instance, noted on the August earnings call that it expects revenue to increase by 70% in fiscal 2028. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress noted that "this is a supply-constrained outlook," suggesting that the company could clock faster growth if it can fulfill more demand. Nvidia's guidance is quite impressive, given that its top line is expected to jump 90% in fiscal 2027 (ending in January next year) to nearly $412 billion.

Even better, the company's earnings per share (EPS) are anticipated to jump by 95% in fiscal 2027, followed by a 71% increase in fiscal 2028. Meanwhile, Broadcom expects its AI revenue to double over the next couple of fiscal years. The incredible demand for Broadcom's custom AI processors and networking chips will push its AI semiconductor revenue to $58 billion in the recently concluded fiscal 2026, up by 186% from the prior year.
The company forecasts $230 billion in AI semiconductor revenue in fiscal 2028, nearly 4x the AI revenue it is poised to generate this year. So, it is easy to see why analysts are anticipating both Nvidia and Broadcom to clock healthy EPS growth over the long run.

Moreover, both stocks are attractively valued following their recent slides, especially when their growth potential is considered. Nvidia has a price/earnings-to-growth ( PEG ) ratio of just 0.27, while Broadcom's PEG ratio is 0.99, according to Morningstar. The PEG ratio is a forward-looking valuation metric that accounts for a company's projected annual earnings growth over the next five years.
A reading below 1 suggests the stock is undervalued relative to its growth potential. So, investors are getting a good deal on these AI stocks that could make them richer in the future. Nvidia's 12-month median price target of $320 implies a 58% jump, while Broadcom's target of $530 suggests 64% gains. As such, buying these top chip stocks right now could prove profitable.
Micron Technology has been seeing exponential growth in revenue and earnings due to the terrific demand for memory chips and the accompanying supply shortage.

The good news is that the favorable memory market dynamics fueling Micron's growth are sustainable. Micron's peer SK Hynix recently noted that the memory shortage won't be going away until 2030, driven by robust demand from AI data centers and emerging AI applications such as humanoids. As a result, SK Hynix estimates that memory demand will continue to outpace supply until the end of the decade.
This is great news for Micron stock investors, especially given that it trades at an attractive 12 times earnings. Micron's 24% share of the dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) market and 15% share of NAND flash storage memory put it in a terrific position to sustain the healthy growth it has been clocking over the past couple of years.
Not surprisingly, Micron has a 12-month median price target of $1,575, implying 89% upside from current levels. The stock could easily outpace analysts' targets over the coming year as it trades at an extremely attractive valuation even though it is expected to deliver long-term EPS growth of 55%, according to YCharts.
As such, savvy investors can consider using Micron's latest pullback to buy a top growth stock trading at an attractive valuation, as it could make them richer over the long term amid the secular growth of the memory market.

articles.title_orig: CVS to split off drugstore business in major breakup of healthcare giant
articles.title_zh: CVS to split off drugstore business in major breakup of healthcare giant
articles.content_orig:
CVS Health plans to split into two separate public companies by the first half 2028 in what would be one of the largest corporate splits in history, the company announced Wednesday.
The move would reverse the company's massive $78 billion acquisition of its insurer, Aetna, and dismantle the vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate it created in 2018. The plan would specifically separate CVS' roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark, one of the nation's three largest PBMs.
The decision follows a "comprehensive strategic review" by the company's board of directors, according to a news release.
It's a stunning reversal for the healthcare powerhouse, which has spent the last two decades working to turn itself into a one-stop health destination. The move also comes as CVS' aggressive turnaround plan under CEO David Joyner shows substantial progress, with the company pursuing $2 billion in cost cuts, store closures, leadership shakeups and efforts to rein in Medicare Advantage costs.
"From a position of strength, and a focus on the long term, we plan to create two focused companies to improve consumer engagement, affordability, and care coordination," Joyner said in the release.
CVS shares have jumped roughly 70% since Joyner took the helm in October 2024, bringing the company's market value to $117 billion.
The two new companies would both be publicly traded.
The insurance and PBM company will retain the CVS Health name and be run by Joyner, while the other company will be called CVS Pharmacy and be led by Prem Shah, who is currently group president of CVS Health. Additional leadership positions and board members will be announced at a later date, CVS said.
Existing CVS shareholders will own shares in both companies after the split. The Financial Times on Tuesday first reported the breakup plans.
The company's pharmacy business raked in $37.66 billion in 2025 sales, while its insurance unit booked $36.29 billion in revenue and healthcare services segment generated $51.24 billion.
CVS on Wednesday also posted third-quarter earnings and revenue that topped Wall Street expectations. Total sales climbed to $108.40 billion, from $102.87 billion in the prior-year period.
Sales were boosted by year-over-year growth in the company's health care benefits and health services segments. Meanwhile, revenue in its pharmacy services business slid from the previous year.
On Wednesday, CVS said it will lump its insurer and PBM with its primary care business Oak Street Health, home-visit provider Signify Health and the company's specialty drug business.
CVS also said the split will allow the two companies to experience a "focused strategic agenda" and greater ability to "innovate, adopt technology, increase efficiency," among other benefits.
It's not the first time CVS has weighed splitting the company. In October 2024, CVS engaged advisors in a strategic review of its business and considered breaking up its retail pharmacy and insurance units.
Even so, Leerink Partners analyst Michael Cherny said the split "feels like a complete shock" in a Tuesday note. But he said that the retail pharmacy business has been performing well, winning market share from competitors and seeing stabilizing gross margins thanks to CostVantage, a new pharmacy reimbursement model introduced by CVS last year.
"In this context, perhaps the outlook for a standalone retail pharmacy (still with meaningful scale and leverage on its own) is stronger now than before," Cherny wrote.
He added that "the rationale could also be to avoid what has been relentless state legislative scrutiny over the company's level of vertical integration."
The potential breakup also comes as pharmacy benefit managers face mounting bipartisan scrutiny in Washington, D.C., and across states.
PBMs, which negotiate drug prices and manage prescription drug benefits on behalf of insurers and employers, have been criticized for opaque pricing practices, their growing market power and potential conflicts of interest when they are owned by companies that also operate insurers and pharmacies.
Congress enacted PBM reforms in February, including provisions to change how PBMs are compensated under Medicare Part D. Meanwhile, states have increasingly moved to restrict PBMs' ownership of pharmacies.

By Purvi Agarwal and Johann M Cherian
Nov 4 (Reuters) - Data center stocks slid in premarket trading on Wednesday, while clean-energy shares rallied after Democrats seized control of Congress, prompting investors to reposition for tougher scrutiny of the AI boom and a shift in ‌policy priorities.
The Democratic sweep, which included victories in traditional Republican strongholds and key data-center hubs Texas and Georgia, will usher in divided government ‌in Washington and raises the prospect of greater congressional oversight of industries that benefited from Republican control.
Market reaction rippled across AI-linked stocks, renewables, healthcare companies, defense contractors and prison operators.
Data ​center operators lost ground, with Core Scientific down 3.5% and Iren down 3.6%. Applied Digital and CoreWeave fell 2.4% and 3.8%, respectively.
The data center boom sparked public backlash this year, raising concerns that tighter Democratic oversight could slow investment just as investors grow wary of soaring AI spending and uncertain returns.
Though analysts doubt any legislation could meaningfully stall data center construction, a Democratic-led Congress increases prospects of more hearings and investigations related to the AI buildout.
"AI has been an enormous engine powering ‌the US economy, so any curbs on its future ⁠development could threaten to put the brakes on growth," said Kit Rees, investment strategist at Quilter.
A Democratic sweep could bolster expectations for continued federal support for clean energy while speeding approvals for energy and infrastructure projects.
Democrats plan to scrutinize the ⁠Trump administration's efforts to roll back emissions rules and could use the Congressional Review Act to overturn regulations that make it easier to sell gas-powered trucks and SUVs.
Shares of solar maker First Solar gained 7%, residential solar installer Sunrun added 6.1% and inverter maker Enphase Energy was up 3.6%. Clean-power developer NextEra Energy inched 2.3% higher.
"The more ​that ​oil and gas prices rise, the bigger the incentive, the bigger the economic incentive to ​roll out clean energy," said Paul Jackson, global market strategist ‌for EMEA at Invesco.
Europe's Vestas and Orsted rose 4.3% and 6.4%, respectively, while Portugal's EDP Renewables was up 2.3%.
Shares of Elon Musk's rocket and space technology company SpaceX dropped 5.2%, while EV maker Tesla was down 4.9%.
"It puts into doubt a potential merger between SpaceX and Tesla. While Congress cannot stop a merger, they could slow it down via extra scrutiny," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB.
"Musk had poured hundreds of millions into the Republican Party ahead of these elections...we could see stocks linked to Musk struggle now that his political enemies have won back control of Congress."
Trump Media & Technology Group, majority-owned ‌by Trump, dropped 7.7%.
Defense contractors such as Northrop Grumman fell 2.7%, while RTX, ​Lockheed Martin and L3Harris lost over 2% each. The sector had been underpinned by expectations that ​the $1.5-trillion budget request by Trump would not face headwinds in a ​Republican-dominated Congress.
However, in a Democrat-led Congress, analysts project the funding could fall short of expectations.
HEALTH INSURERS AND HOSPITAL OPERATORS
Shares of hospital ‌operators such as HCA Healthcare and Universal Health Services gained ​5.4% and 3.4%, respectively.
Insurers such as Centene ​rose 4.7% and Elevance was marginally higher.
Democrats have pushed for universal healthcare policies that could mean more government spending allocated to the sector.
BNP Paribas economist Anis Bensaidani said Democrats may lack the numbers to pass legislation restoring major parts of the Affordable Care Act, but they could ​still win concessions while negotiating over defense spending and ‌government funding.
Prison operators such as GEO Group and CoreCivic fell 6.2% and 5.7%, respectively. The two stocks have rallied sharply since ​Trump won the presidency two years ago, as his clampdown on illegal immigration boosted the need for detention facilities.
(Reporting by Purvi Agarwal ​and Johann M Cherian in Bengaluru; Editing by Shreya Biswas and Anil D'Silva)

articles.title_zh: Dow futures rally 700 points as Democrats win big in midterms: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures ripped higher on Wednesday, reversing earlier losses, as a decisive victory by Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections allowed investors to look past the political risk hanging over the market.
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 724 points, or 1.4%. S&P 500 futures traded 1% higher, along with Nasdaq-100 futures . Stock futures were down sharply overnight.
Democrats took control of Congress Tuesday night, winning majorities in both the House and Senate. They also scored victories in key gubernatorial races, including Texas.
Heading into the election investors worried a Democratic sweep could weigh on some areas of the market , especially stocks related to the artificial intelligence build-out. Wall Street also worried that a clear winner would not emerge Tuesday night. However, those concerns eased after President Donald Trump said he was willing to accept the election results and work with Democrats.
Elon Musk's SpaceX was down 4.8% in premarket trading, while Tesla shares shed 4.9%. Neocloud stocks CoreWeave and Nebius fell 3.6% and 1%, respectively.
But other parts of the tech trade gained. Microsoft advanced 0.3%, and Amazon climbed 1.1%, as Nvidia moved 0.5% higher. Alphabet was the outlier, trading around 0.4% lower.
U.S. health insurers and hospital operators also advanced, with United Health up 1.4%, Molina Healthcare rising 6.3%, Centene adding 4.7% and HCA Healthcare up 1.44%.
Renewables stocks rallied sharply in premarket trading, while defense stocks fell.
AMD shares popped 6% after the chipmaker reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that blew past analyst expectations.
Andrew Slimmon of Morgan Stanley Investment Management said the result will bring "gridlock" to Washington, but added that the markets "like gridlock — they don't like a party with too much power."
Speaking with CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe", Slimmon said that if the result increases the push for a resolution to the Middle East conflict, that may bring oil prices lower.  "That's been an issue for the Fed, and inflation, and part of the reason that rates are higher."
Renewable shares like solar stocks traded higher in the post-market on speculation a Democratic majority in Congress would halt policies by President Donald Trump taken against the industry. The Invesco Solar ETF was up 3% in Robinhood trading.
President Donald Trump may have helped ease pressure on the market a bit overnight by not challenging the midterm results in an interview with the Wall Street Journal . Trump told the WSJ, "I think we'll work with the Democrats, and we'll get along very well with them."
Nasdaq-100 futures are up 929.75 points off their overnight lows, based on the current price of 28,545.50. Futures contracts tied to the benchmark hit a low of 27,615.75,  their lowest since July 30.
Precious metals saw strong gains on Wednesday morning as the Democrats scored a clean sweep in the midterm elections, flipping both the House and Senate.
Spot gold was 2.93% higher at $4,043.45 an ounce by 5:05 a.m. ET, while spot silver jumped 4.44% to trade at $51.98 per ounce, as traders reacted to the U.S. midterm election results.
Front-month gold futures added 2.9% to trade at $4,054.60, while silver futures were up 4.64% at $52.09.
Other metals seeing notable gains on Wednesday morning included platinum , which jumped 2.47% to trade at $1,465.30, and palladium, which was 5.93% higher at $989.
Renewables and healthcare shares are among the biggest premarket movers, trading higher after Democrats took control of the House and Senate. Meanwhile, neocloud stocks, as well as prison operators and defense names, lag the broader market.
U.S. renewable energy stocks climbed on expectations of a policy shift. First Solar advanced 8.5%, Bloom Energy gained 5.8%, Plug Power rose 10.6%, Sunrun notched an 8.64% gain, FuelCell Energy was up 6.24% and SolarEdge Technologies moved 4% higher.
Healthcare stocks also rose. UnitedHealth gained 1.8%, Molina Healthcare added 6.3%, Centene climbed 5% and HCA Healthcare advanced 7.16%.
Neocloud stocks, in contrast, turned lower, with CoreWeave down 3.6% and Nebius off 1%. Shares of prison operators and defense names also fell.
European renewable energy stocks moved sharply higher in early trade as prospects of a decisive Democrat victory in the U.S. midterm elections sparked hopes of a U.S. policy shift on renewables.
Copenhagen-listed Oersted surged 7.3% while Danish peer Vestas advanced 5.2%. The two companies have grappled with uncertainty in their U.S. businesses in recent years, partly as a result of fierce opposition from the Trump administration toward the renewable energy sector.
SMA Solar shares were up 5.5% and Nordex shares added 4.8%.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 added 0.44% in early trading, as the continent's stocks and major bourses moved higher on the Democrats' clean sweep of the U.S. midterms.
Banks advanced 1.83%, leading gains, with basic resources up 1.71% and utilities rising 0.68%. Food and beverage stocks lost 0.57%, and industrial goods fell 0.37%.
The Italian FTSE MIB was up 0.88%, leading regional bourses. The U.K.'s FTSE 100 added 0.22%, while the French CAC 40 rose 0.24% and Germany's DAX gained 0.28%.
Novo posted quarterly earnings ahead of expectations early Wednesday as sales of its Wegovy pill blew past estimates amid continued GLP-1 volume growth globally, sending shares up as much as 6% in early trading.
The company updated its outlook to now see adjusted revenue and operating profit growth between negative 2% and 2% at constant exchange rates. It previously saw full-year sales and operating profits, which it hiked in August, at negative 6% to flat for both metrics.
Sales in the third quarter came in at 79.2 billion Danish kroner ($11.9 billion), up 4% year-on-year at constant exchange rates and ahead of FactSet estimates of 73.6 billion kroner. Adjusted operating profit (EBIT) was 31.7 billion kroner, compared with the expected 28.6 billion kroner.
It comes as the Danish weight-loss drug maker is looking to regain momentum following a tumultuous year in which it fell behind rival Eli Lilly.
Asia-Pacific markets closed mixed Wednesday, as investors assessed a projected Democratic takeover of the U.S. Senate and House, while President Donald Trump appeared to not challenge the results.
"We'll work with the Democrats, and we'll get along very well with them," Trump told the Wall Street Journal.
South Korea's Kospi rose 0.62% to end at 5,683.8, while the small-cap, tech-focused Kosdaq added 1.5% to 714.95 in choppy trading.
Japan's Nikkei 225 pared some losses to close 1.42% lower at 62,188.63, and the broad-based Topix declined 0.89% to 3,895.38.
Mainland China's CSI 300 gained 2.31% to 4,101.34, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was 1.43% higher in its last hour of trade.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 fell 0.59% to 8,834.5.
— Lee Ying Shan, Lim Hui Jie
The dollar moved lower against most major currencies as the Democrats took control of Congress after the U.S. midterm elections.
The euro was last seen 0.39% higher against the dollar at $1.1235, while the British pound also strengthened against the greenback, rising 0.48% to $1.3476.
The dollar index , which tracks the greenback's strength against a basket of six major currencies, was down 0.39% at $101.32.
Treasury yields moved lower on Wednesday as investors sought shelter from a sell-off in equity futures sparked by potential big victories from Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections.

articles.title_orig: U.K. Supreme Court Hears Challenge to Ban on Palestine Action: What to Know
articles.title_zh: U.K. Supreme Court Hears Challenge to Ban on Palestine Action: What to Know
articles.content_orig:
An appeal challenging the designation of Palestine Action as a “terrorist” organisation has begun at the United Kingdom’s top court, as police arrested demonstrators who gathered outside to protest against the group’s proscription.
The two-day hearing at the Supreme Court in London began on Wednesday. Huda Ammori, cofounder of Palestine Action, said ahead of the hearing that she would argue the ban is having a disproportionate effect on freedom of speech and the right to protest.
The direct action group was proscribed by the UK government under then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer in July last year. The decision has since been denounced by rights groups, including Amnesty International and Liberty.
Palestine Action describes itself as a “direct action movement committed to ending global participation in Israel’s genocidal and apartheid regime”. Its designation as a “terrorist” organisation puts it on the same list as armed groups such as al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS). Those found guilty of belonging to or supporting Palestine Action risk up to 14 years in prison.
As the hearing got under way, protesters gathered outside the court. Some expressed support for Palestine Action, while others opposed the group’s proscription, which many view as an affront to civil liberties. One demonstrator held a placard reading: “God help us Jews who support Palestine and Palestine Action”.
About 25 protesters were arrested, according to the Press Association; the final person detained carried a sign saying: “God help us who are not married to the UK’s national security adviser who support Palestine and Palestine action.”
It’s understood this is in reference to journalist and author Sarah Helm, who is married to the UK Prime Minister’s national security adviser, and who had earlier posted a similar line on X but did not face prosecution.
“Today was another demonstration of the chaos wrought by the Government’s grave misuse of terrorism powers to proscribe Palestine Action,” Tom Southerden, Amnesty International’s UK Law and Human Rights Director, said in a statement issued after Wednesday’s arrests.
“The sight of musicians, politicians and celebrities being arrested for peacefully holding placards is a grim one. That they were arrested for using the same language that Sarah Helm didn’t face arrest for, shows how dangerously vague our terrorism laws are.”
Amnesty is one of several organisations calling for the UK government to lift the ban on Palestine Action.
“Whatever the Supreme Court ultimately decides, it’s long past time for the Government to admit they got this badly wrong, end the proscription of Palestine Action and put a stop to these appalling arrests,” Southerden said.
The UK government’s crackdown on pro-Palestine voices has come under intense scrutiny since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza more than three years ago.
Last week, Swedish academic Andreas Malm was prevented from entering the UK after the government said his presence was “not conducive to the public good”. Malm is a vocal supporter of Palestine and has spoken out against Israel’s assault on Gaza.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said before taking office in July that the Labour Party had “got it wrong” on Gaza. However, his comments have come under renewed scrutiny after Malm was refused entry to the UK last week.

articles.title_orig: ASUS announces ROG XG Station 3 with Thunderbolt 5 and RTX 5090 BTF support
articles.title_zh: ASUS announces ROG XG Station 3 with Thunderbolt 5 and RTX 5090 BTF support
articles.content_orig:
External GPU dock supports up to 80 Gbps bandwidth and requires a separate SFX power supply.
ASUS has announced the ROG XG Station 3, an external GPU dock designed for laptops with Thunderbolt 5 connectivity. The device supports desktop graphics cards from the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 50 Series, RTX PRO 6000 Series, AMD Radeon RX 9000 Series and Intel Arc Series. ASUS first demonstrated the dock at Computex 2025, and later showcased it in May this year , but has now issued another announcement with additional details about connectivity and graphics card compatibility.
The ROG XG Station 3 uses Thunderbolt 5 with up to 80 Gbps of bidirectional bandwidth, twice the maximum bandwidth of Thunderbolt 4. It also supports Thunderbolt 5 Bandwidth Boost, which increases bandwidth to 120 Gbps in one direction for display traffic. The dock is backward compatible with Thunderbolt 4 laptops, although these systems will operate at lower connection speeds.
The dock features an open-air design with an integrated GC-HPWR connector for ASUS BTF 2.5 graphics cards. This allows compatible models, including the ROG Astral GeForce RTX 5090 BTF Edition and TUF Gaming GeForce RTX 5080 BTF OC Edition, to receive power without a visible graphics card power cable. Conventional graphics cards are also supported using standard PCIe power connections.
ASUS confirms that the XG Station 3 does not include a power supply. Users must install their own SFX or SFX-L PSU with sufficient capacity for the selected graphics card. The dock supports graphics cards measuring up to 361 × 139.3 × 93.9 mm. The open design provides direct airflow to the graphics card and includes Aura Sync RGB lighting.
The ROG XG Station 3 includes two Thunderbolt 5 ports. The upstream connection provides up to 140W of USB Power Delivery to a compatible laptop. The downstream port supports up to three 4K displays through daisy chaining and offers 36W charging for connected devices. Two additional USB-C 10 Gbps ports are available for peripherals and external storage.
The external GPU dock allows laptop users to connect desktop graphics cards for gaming, content creation and AI workloads. Actual performance will depend on the graphics card, laptop and Thunderbolt connection.
Remember that Thunderbolt 5 still limits PCIe tunneling to 64 Gbps, even though the interface supports up to 80 Gbps of bidirectional bandwidth.

Four oil tankers were destroyed after hitting naval mines in an area south of the Strait of Hormuz proscribed by Iran as prohibited for navigation, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Wednesday, as attacks on vessels in the region intensify while crude oil flows have dipped from recent highs.
The four tankers are still ablaze, while two other vessels have been seized, the Revolutionary Guards said.
While flows have recovered substantially from the lows in the spring, the security situation in and near the Strait of Hormuz has actually deteriorated, with a higher number of attacks on tankers in recent weeks.
Following a post-war peak in September, exports of crude oil, condensate, and fuels from the Middle East slipped to 17.1 million barrels per day (bpd) in October, down from 18.9 million bpd in September, according to data from Vortexa cited by Reuters .
“October data shows Middle East seaborne oil exports have pulled back slightly from recent post-war highs on heightened risks in the Strait of Hormuz,” George Morris, an analyst at Vortexa, said in comments reported by the publication.
Kpler has tracked a 1-million-bpd drop in total crude oil and condensate exports. Crude and condensate flows through the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, and the Gulf of Oman are estimated, provisionally, to have dropped to 16.1 million bpd in October, from 17.09 million bpd in September.
However, the tanker-tracking services caution that the numbers could be revised up as more details on shipments, especially shuttle shipments, emerge in the coming days.
Oil flows from the Middle East region have materially increased since the lows in April and May, but the heightened security concerns and intensified attacks, mines, and other explosions and incidents are making tracking shipments difficult. Tanker-trackers increasingly rely on satellite imagery to confirm movements because vessels are often switching off transponders to avoid detection when transiting the Strait of Hormuz.
